title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
section: Overview of NABat and the NNW Bat Hub
text:
Overview of NABat and the NNW Bat Hub
North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat) is a large-scale coordinated effort to monitor bat species to address gaps in knowledge and lack of long-term studies across North America (Loeb et al. 2015).The program is administered by the US Geological Survey (USGS) and implemented by the North by Northwest Bat (NNW) Hub in British Columbia, Alberta and S.E Alaska.
NNW Bat Hub was established in 2024 with collaboration from Government of British Columbia, Government of Alberta, and Government of Alaska. The hub was formed by combining the previous Alberta Hub and the BC and southeast Alaska (BC-SE_AK) Hub. The implementation of the program within British Columbia has key support from Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCSC), government staff, other wildlife biologists, Indigenous Nations, community members and naturalists across the province.
The centralization of efforts for the hub will expand exciting programs to coordinate more efficiently across jurisdictions, ensuring consistent and long-term bat monitoring through standardized data collection, and streamlined bioacoustic data management. It also seeks to enhance engagement with NABat, foster collaboration among stakeholders, and produce annual reports on regional monitoring.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
section: Threats to bat populations in BC
text:
Threats to bat populations in BC
Bat populations in British Columbia face a wide range of threats including forestry practices, anthropogenic expansion, and climate change among others. A comprehensive review of tese threats and their relative impacts on individual bat species can be found in the BC Bat Action Plan (Team 2024). Of these threats, White-Nose Syndrome and wind energy development have emerged as two of the highest-priority concerns.

White-Nose Syndrome
White-nose Syndrome (WNS) is a deadly fungal disease caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd) that affects hibernating bats. As of 2026, WNS has been confirmed in nine Canadian provinces including Alberta, and Pd has been detected within British Columbia at two locations ( Figure 1: CWHC-RCSF (2024)). Continued monitoring of populations in BC is critical as Pd and WNS continue to spread throughout the province.






Figure 1: White-nose syndrome (WNS) and Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd) occurrence in Canada. Source: CWHC-RCSF (2026)





Wind Energy Development
Wind energy farms has been linked to high mortality rates across all bat species in Canada, with long distance migratory species accounting for 73% of recorded fatalities (Zimmerling and Francis 2016). In British Columbia alone, one estimate predicts an annual mortality rate of 680 bats per wind turbine (Zimmerling and Francis 2016). There are currently close to 300 turbines active in the province across 10 different projects with the most turbines found in the Peace region (Figure 2). In late 2024, B.C announced nine new wind projects which would require the installation of over 300 new wind turbines across the province (Energy and Climate Solutions 2024). As of 2023, COSEWIC designated all three of B.C.’s long distance migratory species as endangered due in part to fatalities at wind turbine facilities (Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada 2023).






Figure 2: Current wind turbines in British Columbia based on the Canadian Wind Turbine Database (Source: https://search.open.canada.ca/openmap/79fdad93-9025-49ad-ba16-c26d718cc070)

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Acoustic Monitoring of Bats
Acoustic recording is a cost-effective method for monitoring bat populations across large geographic and temporal scales. However, several limitations affect the conclusions that can be drawn from these data:

Imperfect species identification — Unlike birds, bats rely on echolocation rather than song, and species with similar ecology and physiology often produce overlapping calls. While detectors are deployed to maximize recordings of diagnostic Search Phase calls, species identifiability will always vary depending on the local assemblage.
Variable detectability — Bat species are not equally detectable acoustically. Larger, wide-ranging species produce louder calls that travel farther, while smaller species with quieter calls or specialized habitat use are less reliably recorded. As a result, trend estimates cannot be produced for all species using acoustic methods alone.
Data variability — Many factors influence recording quality and bat activity, including wind speed, humidity, and local habitat. Additionally, stationary detectors cannot account for individual recapture, meaning acoustic data can only inform relative activity and occupancy.
Processing limitations — Auto-ID software enables efficient processing of large datasets but has known high misclassification rates for bats, making manual verification necessary to ensure accurate results.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Updates in Modelling Approaches
Bat monitoring data can be analyzed using different statistical approaches, each with distinct assumptions and outputs. Activity trend models examine changes in relative acoustic activity over time, providing a straightforward measure of whether bat detections are increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable across the monitoring network.
Dynamic occupancy models take a different approach, estimating the probability that a species occupies a given site while explicitly accounting for imperfect detection. Rather than treating a non-detection as an absence, these models distinguish between a species being truly absent and simply going undetected, an important consideration given the variable detectability of bats discussed above. They also track colonization and extinction probabilities across sites over time, providing insight into range shifts and local population dynamics.
The two approaches differ in sensitivity and therefore serve complementary roles. Activity data are inherently noisy, influenced by weather, local foraging conditions, and the number of individuals passing a detector, but they respond quickly to change and can provide an early indication of decline. Occupancy, in contrast, changes only when a species is lost from (or gains) sites, so a stronger and more sustained signal is needed before a trend becomes apparent. Occupancy models can therefore act as a second, more conservative test of patterns first suggested by activity data. When both approaches point in the same direction, the evidence for a real population change is stronger, and confidence in the results is correspondingly higher.
In 2025, both model types were run to examine differences in results and assess the complementary information each approach provides.

Data Collection
The BC NABat monitoring program was established in 2016 by Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCSC) and has since sampled 65 grid cells. Cells were drawn from the NABat Generalized Random Tessellation Stratified (GRTS) sampling frame (Loeb et al. 2015), and selected based on accessibility, the presence of bat habitat, suitable recorder sites and in GRTS priority order. Where possible, cells were also selected based on the precense of a relatively straight road of 30–45 km for a driving transect.

Stationary Surveys
Two to four stationary detectors were deployed across at least two quadrants per grid cell for a minimum of seven nights. Sites are selected to maximize species detection and recording quality across different habitat types (see Rae and Lausen (2024) for full site selection criteria). Deployment occured between mid-May and mid-July, after bats have emerged from hibernation but before young bats are volant. Sites and timing are kept consistent between years to minimize variability in conditions affecting bat activity.


Transect Surveys
Where possible, driving transects were conducted following Loeb et al. (2015). Two replicates of a 30–35 km route are driven at 30–35 km/h with a rooftop detector, using straight roads that minimize switchbacks. Transects are conducted concurrently with stationary deployments.


Equipment
A wide range of equipment has been used across sampling locations in BC. Until 2024, stationary acoustic units were primarily Wildlife Acoustics SM4Bat-FS or SM2Bat units (Maynard, MA), alongside an increasing number of Titley Scientific Swift and Express units (Brisbane, AU). Mobile transects were conducted using either the Wildlife Acoustics EchoMeter Touch2Pro or Titley Scientific Anabat units (SD1/2 zero-cross or Walkabout models).
2025 represents a transition year for equipment standardization. All SM2Bat units are being replaced with Titley Scientific Chorus units, and Anabat units are being phased out in favour of the EchoMeter Touch2Pro for mobile transects. To account for detection differences between outgoing and incoming equipment, paired deployments were conducted at a number of grid cells this year, both stationary (SM2Bat and Chorus) and mobile (Anabat SD1 and EchoMeter Touch2Pro).


Landscape and Weather Covariates
We used the same covariates for the activity trend models as Rae and Lausen (2022). Where possible, temperature and relative humidity were recorded in each grid cell with onsite data loggers. Where loggers were unavailable, values came from the nearest climate station in the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium (PCIC) Provincial Climate Data Set (PCDS), which aggregates and quality-controls observations from multiple provincial and federal networks. From these station records we also derived nightly mean wind speed (km/h) and nightly total precipitation (mm). Degree days above 10 °C since January 1 were calculated from daily temperature records for each site-night.
Sun and moon positions were calculated with the astral package (v3.2) in Python. Sunset and sunrise times defined the night period for each site-night. Moon illumination was then calculated as the proportion of the lunar disc illuminated multiplied by the proportion of the night the moon spent above the horizon. Site elevation was extracted from the Open-Meteo Elevation API. Distance to clutter and percent clutter were recorded by grid leaders at deployment, and distance to water and water body type were derived from the BC Freshwater Atlas.

For the dynamic occupancy models, we explored additional factors that might influence colonization and extinction: distance to the nearest road and distance to the nearest timber harvest, each measured from the survey location to the closest feature. Road features came from the Human Footprint Index (HFI) layer under development by the Geospatial Centre at Biodiversity Pathways (unpublished data). Harvest features came from the Province of British Columbia’s consolidated cutblocks layer. All continuous covariates were standardized by centering on the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. Missing values were imputed with the global mean before standardization.
Since 2022, insect activity has also been sampled along transect routes using vehicle-mounted sticky traps. Samples are identified to order, and we will evaluate insect abundance as a potential covariate of bat activity in future years.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Acoustic Processing
In 2025 acoustic analysis mostly followed the standards set in previous years (Rae and Lausen 2022, 2024). This included running all files through two automatic classifiers, Kaleidoscope’s Bats of North America 5.4.0 classifier and Sonobat 3.0’s Northwestern British Columbia classifier, to remove files that do not contain bat pulses and giving a preliminary bat species identification.
Manual vetting largely follows the protocol of Reichert et al. (2018a) and previous analysis standards developed by WCSC (Rae and Lausen 2022) . The key difference in the 2024 and 2025 acoustic analysis compared to previous years is that not all automatic species identifications were manually verified. Instead, based on findings from Stratton et al. (2022) , at least 50% of recordings were selected for manual verification.

Subsetting for manual verification
Starting in 2024, the NNW Bat Hub implemented manual vetting of only a subset of all the bioacoustic data collected under the NABat program. Given the project’s large scale, manually vetting all recordings is not feasible long-term. To address this, the NNW Bat Hub, in collaboration with WCSC and contractor Brian Paterson, developed procedures to ensure that selecting a subset of recordings for manual review minimizes biases in analytical results. These standards prioritize the accurate identification of rare and difficult-to-recognize species to maintain the integrity of models and analyses.
To ensure data accuracy, manual verification was conducted based on the number of tagged recordings at each site. For sites with 200 or fewer tagged recordings, all non-noise recordings were manually reviewed. For sites with more than 200 tagged recordings, verification depended on the proportion of recordings assigned a species label. All tags for rare species (comprising ≤10% of prior years’ identifications) and commonly misidentified species were fully vetted. Specifically, all Eastern Red Bat (Lasiurus borealis) tags were manually reviewed due to frequent misclassification as Little Brown Bats (Myotis lucifugus). Additionally, recordings of common species were randomly selected for verification until 50% of total recordings were reviewed. If fewer than 50% of recordings had species tags, all classifier-assigned tags were manually verified, and “NoID” recordings were randomly selected until 50% of all recordings were reviewed.

All models followed the same basic structure, modelling the total number of detected calls as a negative binomial response with log link:
Total detections ~ YearS + log(Sample Nights) + (1|Grid Cell ID/Quadrant) 
+ species specific covariates
Where total detections is the total number of detected calls of a given species at a site in a given year. YearS is the standardized survey year (years since 2016) and provides the estimate of the temporal activity trend. log(Sample Nights) is the natural logarithm of the number of detector-nights and accounts for variation in sampling effort among site-years. The random intercept (1|Grid Cell ID/Quadrant) gives one random intercept per cell, plus one per specific quadrant within a cell. This allow baseline activity to vary among grid cells and the quadrants within them.
Model fit was assessed for each final model using simulation-based scaled residuals from the DHARMa package , with 1,000 simulations per model. For each model, we inspected residual quantile–quantile plots and plots of residuals against predicted values and against each predictor. We also tested residuals for uniformity (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test), dispersion and outliers. Because large sample sizes can make trivial deviations statistically significant, we considered the magnitude of each deviation alongside its p-value (Harrison et al. 2018). Models were considered adequately fitted if no more than one of these three tests was significant (p < 0.05). Where two or more tests were significant, we examined the residual plots and retained a model only if any deviations were small and showed no systematic pattern.
We conducted our statistical analyses at provincial and regional scales. For the regional analyses, we assigned all sampled grid cells to four geographic regions (Southwestern, Southcentral, Southeastern and Northern), each roughly corresponding to a different species set (Figure 3). Model fit was assessed in the same way as for the provicial scale stationary models.

Use of Automated Identification Results in Stationary Trend Analyses
Stationary trend analyses used AutoID classifications from Kaleidoscope Pro. Manual verification was applied only to flag non-bat noise; where manual review suggested a different species than the AutoID label, the original AutoID classification was retained.
This approach was first identified as necessary in 2023 (Rae and Lausen 2022), when analyses of manually verified data revealed a consistent positive trend across all species, this was interpreted as an artifact of reviewer learning over time rather than a true biological signal. As verifier experience increased across years, calls were increasingly assigned to specific species rather than left unidentified, producing an apparent increase in detections independent of actual bat activity. Because this observer effect is difficult to control for statistically, AutoID classifications are now used as the standard for all activity trend analyses, as automated classifiers apply consistent criteria across all years. While AutoID is subject to some misclassification, the error rate is consistent across years and does not confound detection of genuine temporal trends.



Transect Models
The province-wide transect abundance trend models used only completly manually verified detections. Transects are surveyed from a moving vehicle, so each bat is likely recorded only once as the vehicle passes. Call counts therefore serve as an index of relative abundance rather than of activity. When a detection was identified as a species couplet, it was counted toward each species in the couplet.
All models had the same basic structure: total detections were modelled as a negative binomial response with a log link:
Total detections ~ YearS + log(transect length) + (1|Grid Cell ID) 
+ species specific covariates
Total detections is the number of calls of a given species detected on a transect in a given year. YearS is survey year expressed as years since 2016, and provides the estimate of the temporal activity trend. log(transect length) is the natural logarithm of the total length of the transect sampled and accounts for variation in sampling effort among transects. The random intercept (1|Grid Cell ID) allow baseline activity to vary among grid cells.
Covariates were limited to weather variables, because landscape-level covariates cannot be represented meaningfully for a survey that moves through the landscape. Species-specific covariates for transect models were selected based on those previously established in Rae and Lausen (2022) and were selected using AIC-based stepwise selection (Table 4). Model fit was assessed in the same way as for the stationary models.
Since transects are only conducted in roughly 50% of our grid cells on a typical year and each transect records fewer bats per night than stationary monitoring, we have elected not to conduct regional-scale transect trend analyses due to low sample sizes.

Dynamic Occupancy
We fitted multi-season (dynamic) occupancy models (MacKenzie et al. 2003) to estimate trends in occupancy, colonization, and persistence while accounting for imperfect detection. This analysis used nightly acoustic detection/non-detection data from passive bat detectors deployed at all the sites in British Columbia (BC).
Initial occupancy (\(\psi\)) was modeled as a function of distance to water and elevation. Colonization (\(\gamma\)) and persistence (\(\varphi\)) were modeled as a function of distance to water, elevation, year-varying distance to harvest, and distance to road. Detection probability (p) was modeled as a function of percent clutter, nightly mean temperature, and Julian night. 
We excluded 2016 because few sites were surveyed that year. Starting the time series in 2016 would have required the model to estimate initial occupancy (ψ₁) for the many sites not yet sampled, and a poorly informed ψ₁ can propagate through the colonization and extinction estimates and produce false trends.
To reduce temporal autocorrelation between consecutive nights, we subsampled every other night, using a maximum of four nights per site-year as repeat surveys. Sites were included if they had at least two nights of data in a given year and data from at least two years. After filtering, 185 sites in 63 grid cells in British Columbia were retained. Models were fit separately for each of the 15 bat species.
Models were fit in a Bayesian framework using JAGS (Version 4.3.2) via the jagsUI package (Version 1.6.3) in r (Version 4.5.1). We ran 3 chains in parallel for 30,000 iterations each, discarding the first 15,000 as burn-in and thinning the remainder by 10, yielding 4,500 posterior samples for inference. Priors on all regression coefficients, including region-specific intercepts, were normal with mean 0 and precision 0.368 (SD ≈ 1.65 on the logit scale). Standard deviations of the year-level random effects on colonization, persistence, and detection were assigned half-Cauchy(0, 2.5) priors.
Convergence was assessed using Rhat diagnostics, with values below 1.1 taken to indicate convergence. Results are summarized using posterior means and 95% Bayesian credible intervals. We calculated an overall occupancy trend metric (𝜆) as the ratio of estimated occupancy in the final year to that in the initial year; values of 𝜆 > 1 with 95% credible intervals entirely above 1 indicate an increase in occupancy, values 𝜆<1 with intervals entirely below 1 indicate a decline, and intervals overlapping 1 indicate an uncertain or stable.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Species Detection
All 15 species monitored by the program were detected in 2025. Total acoustic activity varied substantially among grid cells and regions (Figure 3). Little brown myotis and silver-haired bat remain two of the most widespread species in the province. Notable changes in 2025 include:

Pallid bat was detected at only one site, in each of 2023 and 2024. In 2025 it was detected at 14 sites across 6 grid cells, its highest site count since monitoring began and slightly above 2022 (13 sites across 6 grid cells). Pallid bat was first recorded in the Kootenay Region in 2022 and was not detected there in 2023 or 2024. In 2025 it was detected at 8 Kootenay sites across 4 grid cells. Two of these grid cells (111466 and 243562) had no previous detections.
Eastern red bat was detected at 35 sites across 17 grid cells in 2025. That is its highest site count to date, although it was found in more grid cells in 2022 (21). Four grid cells had no previous detections: 111466 and 243562 (Kootenay), 194666 (Okanagan) and 186330 (Northern). Eastern red bat was not detected in the South Coastal Region in 2025.
Northern myotis was detected at 15 sites across 10 grid cells in 2025. In the southern Kootenay Region it was detected for the first time at 4 sites across 3 grid cells (20330, 89962 and 218282), near the southern edge of its range.
Long-legged myotis was detected at 76 sites across 39 grid cells in 2025, down from 92 sites across 45 grid cells in 2023 (the highest year of detection for the species). Most of these losses were in the Okanagan Region (8 sites, 5 grid cells) and the South Coastal Region (5 sites, 2 grid cells). The remaining losses were in the Kootenay and Northern regions (3 sites and 1 grid cell each).

Figure 3 is an interactive map. Readers can zoom in to see the individual stationary monitoring sites (blue circles), and click a site to open a pop-up with a summary pie chart of total detections by species and year. Readers can also search for specific grid cells using the  icon.








Figure 3: Acoustic bat monitoring sites in British Columbia, 2016–2025. Regions were defined by Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCSC) from species range maps to group areas with similar species composition.Click any site to view a summary of species detections by year. Summaries include manually verified detections and automated identifications where two auto-ID programs agreed on the species.

Because these assumptions were not fully met, the magnitudes of the estimated trends should be interpreted with caution, and we therefore focus on trend direction throughout. At the provincial scale, no species showed a significant negative trend in either the stationary or the transect models. Stationary activity increased significantly for five species: pallid bat, Townsend’s big-eared bat, big brown bat, long-eared Myotis and Yuma Myotis (Table 5) . Most of the remaining regional trends were not significant (Table 6). The Kootenay and South Coastal regions had the most significant trends, all of them positive. In the South Coastal region, activity increased for five species (Townsend’s big-eared bat, big brown bat, California Myotis, long-eared Myotis and Yuma Myotis). Big brown bat also increased in the Okanagan region. The only significant negative regional trend was for Yuma Myotis in the Northern region.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Dynamic Occupancy Models
We assessed occupancy trends in two ways: the mean yearly change in occupancy across 2017–2025, and the posterior probability that occupancy in 2025 was higher than in 2017. We considered a posterior probability above 0.95 to be strong evidence of an increase, and one below 0.05 to be strong evidence of a decline.
Overall, occupancy increased across British Columbia between 2017 and 2025 for four of the 15 species modelled (Figure 4). Western long-eared Myotis, little brown Myotis, northern Myotis and silver-haired bat all showed a positive mean yearly trend and a high posterior probability of an increase in occupancy from 2017 to 2025, indicating strong evidence of an overall increase. Fringed Myotis was the only species with a consistent decrease in occupancy: its mean yearly change was negative, and the posterior probability that 2025 occupancy exceeded 2017 occupancy was very low, indicating strong evidence of a decline.
Yuma Myotis, western small-footed Myotis, spotted bat, pallid bat and hoary bat showed no detectable occupancy trend. Their mean yearly change was not significant, and the posterior probability of an increase from 2017 to 2025 gave no clear evidence of either an increase or a decline.
Big brown bat showed no significant mean yearly change, but the posterior probability of an increase between 2017 and 2025 was low, which points to a decline over that period. This was driven by a high posterior mean occupancy in the first year and a slightly below-average posterior mean in the last year (Appendix A), so it more likely reflects a stable population with an unusually high starting point than a true decline.
Eastern red bat, long-legged Myotis, Townsend’s big-eared bat and California Myotis had positive mean yearly trends. However, the posterior probability that occupancy was higher in 2025 than in 2017 was not high enough to conclude that occupancy increased overall. This pattern reflects nonlinear change across years (see species specific results in Appendix A). Occupancy fluctuated enough to produce a positive mean yearly trend, but the net difference between the first and last years was small, suggesting these species remained relatively stable over the monitoring period.






Figure 4: Estimated occupancy trends for 15 bat species in British Columbia (2017–2025) fit across all monitoring sites. Points and bars show the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the linear change in occupancy per year. The dashed line marks zero, where there is no change in mean yearly opccupancy. Colour shows the posterior probability (at ≥ 0.95) that the occupancy in 2025 was higher (green) or lower (red) than in 2017 . Grey means the probability is uncertain. Slope and colour can disagree when trends are non-linear.



Among the regional models, the Kootenay Region showed the most positive trends ( Figure 5). Eastern red bat, silver-haired bat, western small-footed Myotis, western long-eared Myotis, little brown Myotis and long-legged Myotis all had a positive mean yearly trend and a high posterior probability of an increase in occupancy from 2017 to 2025.
In the Northern Region, big brown bat had a negative mean yearly trend and a low posterior probability of an increase, indicating a decline. Eastern red bat also had a low posterior probability of an increase, although its mean yearly change was not significant.
In the Okanagan Region, Townsend’s big-eared bat and eastern red bat had positive mean yearly trends and high posterior probabilities of an increase. Fringed Myotis declined, with both a negative mean yearly trend and a low posterior probability of an increase. Yuma Myotis also had a low posterior probability of an increase, although its mean yearly change was not significant.
In the South Coastal Region, hoary bat had a negative mean yearly trend and a low posterior probability of an increase. Silver-haired bat, California Myotis, western long-eared Myotis and Yuma Myotis had positive mean yearly trends and high posterior probabilities of an increase.






Figure 5: Regional estimated occupancy trends for 15 bat species in British Columbia (2017–2025). Points and bars show the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the linear change in occupancy per year. The dashed line marks zero, where there is no change in mean yearly occupancy. Colour shows the posterior probability (at ≥ 0.95) that the occupancy in 2025 was higher (green) or lower (red) than in 2017 . Grey means the probability is uncertain. Slope and colour can disagree when trends are non-linear.



To show how occupancy varied across space and time, we mapped the model-estimated probability of occupancy at each site for every year from 2017 to 2025 (Figure 6). The map lets readers select a species and move through the years to see where occupancy has changed. Each point’s colour shows the model’s estimate of for yearly probability of occupancy, while its shape shows whether the species was detected that year (circle) or not (triangle). Because the occupancy model accounts for imperfect detection, a site where a species was not detected can still have a high estimated probability of occupancy. This is especially likely for species that are hard to detect acoustically, or at sites with few survey nights in a given year. The map therefore shows where a species was likely present, not just where it was recorded.








Figure 6: Probability of occupancy per site by year for 15 bat species in British Columbia with reliable occupancy estimates. Use the buttons to switch species and the slider to change year. Circles = detected; triangles = not detected that year; colour = model inference for probability of occupancy.




Because the dynamic occupancy model estimates detection probability separately for each year, it also shows how detectability changed over the monitoring period for each species. This lets us account for changes in sampling and processing, such as the equipment change in 2025, so that shifts in detectability are not mistaken for changes in occupancy. The species-specific results (Appendix A) show that the probability of detecting pallid bat and eastern red bat increased in 2025, whereas detection probability for all other species stayed within its normal year-to-year variation.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Species Ranges
Species ranges across the project period (2016–2025) remain broadly stable, with no grid cells showing conspicuous or sustained absences of previously detected species. In 2025 there was a normal variation in the disctribution of species detections across the province, but three species are worth highlighting:

Northern Myotis was detected for the first time in three grid cells (20330, 218282, and 89962) in the southern Kootenay region. These cells lie at the southern edge of the species’ known range, and the detections may indicate a small range expansion. Capture or genetic (guano) surveys will be needed to confirm its presence.
Long-legged myotis was detected at fewer sites in 2025 (76 sites across 39 grid cells) than in 2024 (85 sites across 42 grid cells). Most of the decline was in the South Coastal Region: among sites surveyed in both years, detections fell from 18 sites to 12, with 7 sites losing the species and 1 gaining it. Year-to-year turnover in site-level detections is common for most species in the program, so this decline likely reflects natural variation rather than a population change. However, the proportion of sites with detections has now declined for two consecutive years, so this species should be monitored closely in future years.
Eastern red bat detections increased in the Kootenay and Okanagan regions in 2025. The species was detected in 17 grid cells, the most to date, including four with no previous detections (111466, 243562, 194666, and 186330). Although many knowledge gaps remain for this species, these results continue to support a westward range expansion (Solick et al. 2020). In contrast, eastern red bat was not detected in the South Coastal Region in 2025 after being recorded there every year from 2021 to 2024. Its calls overlap substantially with those of little brown Myotis, making diagnostic recordings difficult to obtain, so this apparent absence may partly reflect the difficulty of confirming the species acoustically rather than a true loss.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Trend analyses
In 2025, we used two complementary analyses to assess population trends. Dynamic occupancy models estimate how the proportion of sites occupied by each species changes over time, while accounting for imperfect detection (the chance that a species is present at a site but not recorded). Activity trend analyses estimate changes in the number of bat passes recorded per night, which reflects how heavily sites are used. Because the two analyses capture different aspects of population change, agreement between them strengthens confidence in the results.
Acoustic data suggest that bat populations in BC are generally stable. Across both analyses, most species showed no discernible trend. Four species (pallid bat, Townsend’s big-eared bat, big brown bat, and Yuma Myotis) showed positive trends in activity but no trend in occupancy (Table 7). This pattern suggests that activity is increasing at sites where these species already occur, rather than the species occupying new sites. These species may be increasing, but confirming this will require positive activity trends sustained over several more years, ideally accompanied by a positive occupancy trend.




Table 7: Summary of provincial-scale population trends for bat species in British Columbia. Activity and transect trends are based on the year coefficient (2016-2025) from models of nightly stationary and mobile transect activity, with increases or decreases identified at p < 0.05. Dynamic occupancy trends are based on the change in occupancy probability between the first and last survey year across all sites (2017-2025), with increases or decreases identified when the 95% credible interval excluded zero. “Not assessed” indicates species that were excluded from, or not modelled in, a given analysis.

Little brown Myotis showed a positive trend in transect activity ( Table 5 ) and an overall increase in occupancy (Figure 4; Appendix A), suggesting the species is increasing across the province. However, Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd), the fungus that causes white-nose syndrome (WNS), was confirmed in the South Coastal Region in 2026 (Kellner, pers. comm.), so this trend is likely to change in coming years. Continued monitoring will be essential for detecting the effects of WNS on this species in BC.
Long-eared Myotis increased in both stationary acoustic activity and occupancy (Table 5;Figure 4), with increases in both analyses concentrated in the Kootenay and South Coastal regions. The reason for this increase is unclear, and it may be partly an artifact of detection. Detection probability for this species was higher from 2023 to 2025 than from 2017 to 2022 (Appendix A), which suggests that something changed in 2023 that made the species easier to detect. Equipment updates are the most likely cause. If equipment changes can be ruled out, a closer look at changes in the Kootenay and South Coastal regions in this period is needed to help explain the increase.
Silver-haired bat may also be increasing in the Kootenay and South Coastal regions, although this is based on occupancy results alone (Table 5; Figure 4). A similar increase in occupancy has been reported for this species in Southeast Alaska (Hurtado and Hart 2026). This trend warrants close monitoring, particularly given planned increases in wind energy development in northern BC.
Fringed Myotis showed no trend in activity but declined in occupancy, driven primarily by a decrease in the Okanagan Region. Continued monitoring will be needed to confirm this decline and to help identify potential causes. Lile et al. (2026) found that the number of Myotis species captured has declined since the arrival of WNS in South Dakota, and fringed Myotis was among the species with significantly fewer captures. A decline in fringed Myotis is therefore a concern: if the species is already decreasing before WNS becomes established in BC, the disease could accelerate that

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Challenges and Lessons Learned

Timing of Data Retrieval and Submission
Field crews across British Columbia continue to reliably collect recordings for their grid cells. However, organizing and submitting these recordings, along with associated metadata, remains a challenge. Delays in data submission from grid leaders extend processing and analysis times, making it difficult to complete reports by the end of the fiscal year. The transition in project management this year further complicated data submission. We anticipate these challenges will be resolved in future years as teams adjust to the new process. To improve efficiency, we plan to increase reminders to grid leaders and provide additional support to address ongoing challenges in data organization and submission.

title: North American Bat Monitoring Program in British Columbia
text:
Looking Forward
The BC NABat program has yielded a large and robust acoustic dataset that provides solid baseline information on distribution of 15 resident BC bat species. The data that has been collected so far are an invaluable reference point for BC’s bat distributions and activity that improve with each additional year of monitoring. Key considerations for the future of the program include:

Manual Verification Efficiency. For many years, the program manually verified 100% of acoustic recordings. As the program continues to expand, this level of effort is no longer sustainable, and manual vetting was reduced to 50% of recordings following the results of (stratton2022?). Since 2023, manual verification has been used only to confirm species presence, while activity metrics are based on automated Kaleidoscope classifications. For the occupancy analyses, manual verification is only needed to confirm species presence at each site and to remove false positive IDs. The additional verification the program currently completes is valuable for maintaining a clean dataset that can be used to evaluate how vetting effort affects results, as it already has been in (stratton2022?). However, it is not required for the analyses presented in this report. If the program needs to find efficiencies, reducing manual verification to the level required for occupancy analyses should be considered
Efficiencies in monitoring. Grid leaders should continue to be encouraged to use Survey123 to streamline site deployment; in 2024 and 2025 this platform was not used consistently across all grids. Using it also helps ensure that metadata are consistent and complete. In 2026 we can also examine efficiencies in weather data collection, specifically evaluating whether continued use of on-site temperature and humidity loggers yields results comparable to weather data drawn from the nearest weather stations.
Adding and maintaining grid cells. Changes in priorities and budgets have reduced repeat visits at some grid cells across the province. Supporting continued sampling at established grid cells is key to tracking population changes over time, especially given the imminent threat of WNS. Collaboration with other agencies and organizations can help sustain monitoring at existing grid cells and expand it to new ones. One approach being explored by the NNW Bat Hub is engaging industry partners, such as those in the mining, forestry, and wind energy sectors, in coordinated monitoring within their operating areas, with data contributed both to the hub and to the broader NABat effort. These partnerships may be easier to establish where regulatory frameworks support them, for example by requiring that bat monitoring data collected for industry projects be submitted to the hub and NABat.
